lines.note: Continues the preceding entry's reference to sleeves, then gives nuqiiredo wo suru, putting one's hands inside the breast of the garment. The scan supports mangas and Meter, not the OCR's mengas and Metes; the enlarged Japanese spelling shows ij before redo, including a descending j, rather than the OCR's single i.
Completes Meter: putting the hands into the bosom in this manner. The printed mãos and historical ſeyo are retained without modernization.
Nukimochi means holding a sword drawn. The principal parts match motsu/motta; arran continues as cada below, with no visible terminal hyphen on this row.
Completes arrancada and illustrates the sense with katana wo nuki motsu. The visible space between nuqi and motçu is retained.
Nukinde, nukinzuru, nukindeta means surpassing or standing out. The Portuguese starts the comparison that continues with a todos below.
The example concerns outstanding loyal service, chūsetsu wo nukinzuru. The final Aſ- begins the Portuguese verb on the next physical row; the caron over u is retained.

runs.text: ſinalarſe em fazer ſeruiços ao ſenhor. ¶

lines.note: Completes the explanation as distinguishing oneself in service to a lord. Gũ- begins the next Japanese example and is upright, not an isolated italic nasal vowel.
With Gũ- above, gunchū wo nukinzuru concerns distinction in military service. The scan reads chǔuo, not the malformed OCR chǔuto; retain the printed single-s spelling Aſinalarſe.

runs.text: tajarſe aos outros no ſeruiço da guera.

lines.note: Completes auentajarſe: surpassing others in war service. The source's guera has one r here and is not silently regularized to guerra.
Nukisashi describes taking out and putting in. The historical aita principal part belongs to the s-verb paradigm and should not be replaced by a modern shita ending.

runs.text: tranca de porta, &c. ou arrancar, & em-

lines.note: Gives a door bar as one object moved in and out, then turns to drawing and sheathing. The printed em- continues directly into bainhar below.
Completes embainhar espada, sheathing a sword, as the second illustration of nukisashi. This is a continuation, not another headword.
Nukisobame means carrying the drawn sword close beside oneself. The final ou is present in the scan but absent from the draft; de ſi is the reflexive phrase.

runs.text: à ilharga a eſpada desembainhada em feição

lines.note: Specifies holding the unsheathed sword at one's flank, in a position described on the next row. The historical Portuguese vocabulary and the short s in desembainhada are preserved.
Completes the posture description: ready to strike or wound. It belongs to nukisobame rather than the following partial-drawing verb.
Nukisukashi is drawing out a little, here specifically a sword. Hum pouco qualifies the extent of the drawing, not the size of the weapon.
Supplies the object of arrancar hum pouco: the sword. The short continuation completes the preceding entry.
Nukisute combines drawing or pulling out with throwing away. The printed tçuru is the historical inflection supplied by the dictionary.
Fora completes lançar fora, throwing away after pulling out. It is the end of the nukisute definition.
Nukitsure means drawing swords together. The nasal abbreviation in jũ- belongs to the Portuguese juntos, completed below.
Begins a battle example: raising a collective battle cry, then referring to the horses' bits in the divided cutçubami. The quotation continues across the next two rows.
Describes aligning the horses, drawing together, and shouting. Cutçubami and coſô are physically divided across rows; the text is not joined in the transcription.
Ends the Japanese account of charging with a shout. Tai. is the upright source label; the scan clearly gives book 14, not OCR book 1, before the Portuguese translation begins.

runs.text: nal de arremeter vnindo, ou igualando os ca-

lines.note: Completes sinal and explains giving the charge signal while bringing the horses abreast. The final ca- begins caualos on the next row.
Completes caualos and describes drawing together before charging. The Portuguese past narrative is retained as printed, including arremeterão.
Ends the battle quotation's translation with a noisy collective shout. This closes the nukitsure example before the new sword-performance entry.

runs.text: Arte de menear a eſpada nua de mui-

lines.note: Nukite is defined here as the art of manipulating a bare sword. The definition concerns performance or dexterity, not simply the modern literal idea of drawing a hand.

runs.text: tas maneiras como fazem os tregeitadores.

lines.note: Completes muitas maneiras and compares the movements to those of performers or jugglers. Tregeitadores is the source's historical spelling.
Nukite no jōzu is a skilled practitioner of this sword art. The caron in jǒzu and the printed destro are retained.
Finishes the skilled-performer gloss and introduces learning the art, nukite wo narau. The source's contracted narǒ is not modernized.
Completes aprender esta arte, then gives nukite wo suru, practising it. The Portuguese Vſar continues onto the next row.
Completes the explanation of practising this art. This short row closes the cluster of nukite examples.
Nukitori means removing by pulling out. The following examples distinguish selected weeds or hairs from the surrounding material.

runs.text: eruas dantre o trigo, ou arroz, cabelos bran-

lines.note: Gives weeds among wheat or rice and begins the example of white hairs. Dantre is the printed historical contraction and bran- continues below.
Completes brancos: plucking white hairs from among black ones. This parallels removing weeds from a crop.

runs.text: Enganos, ou obras com que hum

lines.note: Nukiwaza is glossed as tricks or deceptive actions. The phrase com que hum introduces the person who deceives others on the following row.
Finishes the deception gloss and illustrates nukiwaza wo suru, performing such tricks. Vt is italic apparatus; the example is upright Japanese.
Nurarinurari to describes a slipping or gliding manner. The repeated Japanese stem agrees with the snake comparison that follows.

runs.text: ou ir brandamente como cobra, &c. ¶ Itẽ,

lines.note: Explains smooth movement like a snake, then introduces another sense. The nasal abbreviation Itẽ is preserved rather than expanded to Item.

runs.text: modo de fazer as couſas com priguiça, & ti-

lines.note: The second sense is doing things lazily and without energy. Ti- begins the Portuguese adverb completed below.
Completes tibiamente, reinforcing the languid or half-hearted manner. It remains a physical continuation of the same adverb entry.
Nurashi is the transitive verb 'to wet'. The example begins sode wo nurasu, wetting one's sleeves, which receives a poetic explanation below.

Completes nurasu and glosses the wet-sleeve expression as weeping. P. marks poetic usage. Native enlargement in the second pass confirms that this label is italic with Chorar, so the baseline typeface ownership is retained.
Nure is the intransitive counterpart: becoming wet. The Portuguese reflexive molhar-se makes the contrast with nurashi explicit.
Nurekakari is used here for a coaxing, affectionate manner, not literal wetness alone. The following gloss explains the social behavior meant.

runs.text: como custumão as molheres pera pedir, ou al-

lines.note: The historical gloss describes women making requests or seeking something. This reports the dictionary's wording rather than endorsing its generalization; al- continues into alcançar.

runs.text: cançar algũa couſa com afagos, & meiguices.

lines.note: Completes alcançar and specifies obtaining something through affection and caresses. The entry continues at the top of the second column.

runs.text: Tambem às vezes ſe acommoda aos homẽs.

lines.note: Adds that nurekakari can also be applied to men. This belongs to the entry begun at the bottom of column 1, not to nurefitari below.
Nurehitari means becoming thoroughly wet or soaked. The Japanese fitari corresponds to the hitaru element; en- begins ensopar-se below.
Completes ensoparſe em agoa, becoming soaked in water. The historical spelling agoa is retained.
Nureginu is explained as falsehood or false accusation, with soragoto as a Japanese synonym. The synonym after i, is not a Japanese term embedded in Portuguese prose.
Completes falso testemunho, then gives nureginu wo ou, bearing a false accusation. The circumflex in vô is retained from the print.

runs.text: imposto a alguem crime, ou falta falſamente q̃

lines.note: Explains falsely assigning someone a crime or fault. The final q̃ abbreviates que and is not expanded in the diplomatic text.
Specifies that the wrongful act was committed by someone else. This completes the false-accusation explanation.

runs.text: Eſcrauo, ou peßoa baixa de ſeruiço.

lines.note: Nurei denotes a slave or low-ranking servant in the dictionary's terminology. The scan supports the complete Eſcrauo and peßoa forms.
Nurenezumi is literally a wet rat. The following example applies this comparison to someone thoroughly drenched.
Completes nure-nezumi no yō ni natta, becoming like a wet rat. The scan reads yǒni, not OCR yǒnri, removing the spurious r without changing the long-o mark.
Completes the Portuguese comparison to a wet rat. This closes the drenched-appearance example.
Nuresagi is a flower name here, glossed only as flowers so called. The entry does not warrant a more precise botanical identification from this page alone.
Nuretōri means being wet through to the flesh. The scan's compressed atèa is retained rather than imposing modern word spacing.
Hada made nuretōru illustrates being soaked through to the skin. The f in Fada is the ordinary Jesuit h-row spelling, not a long s.
Nuri, nuru, nutta covers coating, anointing, or lacquering. The principal part utta has the expected double t visible in the scan.
Kabe wo nuru means plastering a wall. The final upright V- begins Vruxide on the next row; it is Japanese text rather than part of the italic gloss.

runs.text: ruxide monouo nuru, l, vruxiuo nuru.

lines.note: Gives two alternatives for coating something with lacquer: urushi de mono wo nuru and urushi wo nuru. The printed l is the Latin alternative marker, not a Japanese syllable.
The Portuguese explains lacquering something, then starts a new example with shigai, a corpse. Vruxar is a Portuguese-derived verb here and remains italic.
With Xigai above, this means applying oil to a dead body. The final cor- starts corpo in the translation below.
Completes corpo morto, the object being anointed. This closes the nuri example series.
Nuribuchi denotes lacquered strips or framing pieces. The gloss's Vruxadas is a Portuguese adjective derived from the lacquer term and is printed italic.
Nurikabe is a plastered wall, directly matching parede barrada. This is an independent nominal entry after the general coating verb.
Nurigasa is a lacquered hat or sunshade. The exact object is described by the historical Portuguese sombreiro, without a modern narrowing in the transcription.
Nurigomedō names a particular lacquered bow. The headword's circumflex is visible; the construction is further specified on the next row.
Completes the bow description as bound with rattan or cane. Rota is the source's material term, not an instruction to normalize it to another spelling.
Nurimono is a lacquered object or lacquerware. The definition is intentionally broad and should not be restricted to a particular vessel.

runs.text: Hum certo vaſo vruxado, ſobre o

lines.note: Nurioke is a particular lacquered vessel. The following row describes the work performed over it rather than giving another object name.

runs.text: qual eſcarpeã, & concertão borra as molheres.

lines.note: Describes women teasing out and arranging fibrous waste or floss over the vessel. The printed eſcarpeã, with its final-a tilde, is retained instead of being regularized to a modern verb form.

runs.text: Caſa que tẽ o telhado por fora barrado.

lines.note: Nuriya is described as a house whose roof is plastered on the outside. The explanation specifically says telhado, so the note does not substitute the more familiar wall-based description.
Nurude no ki names a tree, with no further botanical details in this entry. Preserve the joined aßichamada rather than adding an editorial word space.
Nurui means lukewarm, illustrated with water and wine. The primary temperature sense is distinguished from the figurative sense below.
Adds the figurative meaning tepid, weak, or slack. Per met. is printed explanatory apparatus and is not expanded in the transcription.
Gives the contracted adverbial form corresponding to nurui. The caron over u is visible; no separate Portuguese gloss is printed on this row.
Gives the -sa noun, the quality or degree of being lukewarm or slack. Its indentation associates it with nurui above.
Nurunuru to is glossed as acting tepidly or coldly. The repeated form is a separate adverb entry, not a duplicate of the inflections above.
Nusubito means thief. The long s in the Japanese headword is preserved.
Nusudachi describes game birds taking cover. Only the two printed principal forms are supplied; no missing past tense is invented.

runs.text: ou galinhas do mato por ãtre as eruas, ou ma-

lines.note: Specifies partridges or wild fowl retreating among grass or scrub. The scan has ãtre, with a nasal abbreviation omitted by OCR atre; ma- begins mato below.

runs.text: to com medo dos falcoẽs, & dos caçadores.

lines.note: Explains that the birds hide from falcons and hunters. Native enlargement places the nasal mark on e in falcoẽs; that printed placement is retained rather than normalized to modern falcões.
Nusudo is another word for thief, separately entered from nusubito. Its shorter form is not an OCR omission to be filled from the earlier headword.
Nusumi, nusumu, nusunda is the verb 'to steal'. The scan shows a tilde over the u in ũda, supplying the nasal abbreviation lost by OCR uda.
The same stem is separately entered as the noun theft. The Portuguese noun Furto distinguishes it from Furtar above.
Nusumi idashi means taking or bringing out secretly or by stealing. The visible separation of Nuſumi and idaxi is preserved.

runs.text: como gente pera vender, ou filha dalguem pera

lines.note: Gives the historical examples of carrying off people for sale or someone's daughter. The note reports the dictionary's examples without treating them as ordinary acceptable conduct.

runs.text: ſe caſar a furto, &c. ¶ Item, Alicubi,

lines.note: Completes the example of a clandestine marriage, then introduces a locally restricted additional meaning. Alicubi is a usage limitation, not a place name.

runs.text: no Cami, Enterrar denoite o corpo morto pera

lines.note: In some places in Cami, the expression means burying a body at night. Cami is a Japanese regional designation embedded in Portuguese and is eligible for the optional typeface-term review.
Completes the night-burial explanation: avoiding ceremony and expense. The bottom-right Nuſu- is a catchword and is not a continuation of this sentence.
